rv.q: It’s halfway between a tribute to and a very, very silly send-up of a much-loved movie, whose cava-swilling fans will leave the theatre with a skip, slide and hop in their step.
Amid the numerous laughs and sugary storylines, an oldish man in front of me sucked his gums while gawping at acres of upper leg flesh being displayed by the female dancers.

But if you get on board with its outrageous camp and gurning humour, the tale of the maverick ballroom dancer who just wants to do his own steps – and the shy young Spanish dancer he takes on as his rookie partner – is also loads of fun.
The problem with this, however, and with pushing several performances into caricature, is that it hammers home the irony.
Some persuasive moments, but overall it’s strictly so-so.
Yet despite the meticulous replication, gone is the easy charm of the film, to be replaced by a slightly desperate air of forced jollity beneath the amply applied fake tan.

The saddest thing about DrewMcOnie’s prod- uction is that this gifted choreog- rapher offers endless twiddles of dance, but no exhilarating big numbers. The jukebox score is crooned by the sherry-toned WillYoung, the show’s roller-skating MC.
It's so keen to be a glossy West End show that it loses its heart.
I find more fun in Wagner than in this laborious attempt to turn a charming 1992 movie into a fully fledged stage musical.
It is so lacking in substance that it almost makes its predecessor at this theatre, Annie, look like the Ring Cycle by comparison.
The Musical is a riotous romp for all the senses.
His choreography throughout is sensational and inventive; his direction fluent, keeping control of the frenzy.

Having travelled across Sydney, Leeds, and Toronto on its extensively revised way to the West End , director-choreographer Drew McOnie's musical adaptation of Baz Luhrmann's enjoyably whacked-out film emerges as an overextended and bloated cartoon.
There's hardly room for this disappointingly flaccid and ultimately tacky spectacle.
It seems as if this ballroom blitz is destined to be a West End crowd-pleaser.
Director and choreographer Drew McOnie delivers some stunning dance numbers and negotiates his cast around a very crowded stage which includes a drop-dead-fabulous band.
Whether or not one agrees with Wally that 'Life's three most important things' are 'love, freedom and sequins', the show is a total delight.
But while the story of Scott’s attempt to break free of the conventions of ballroom dancing has heart, only once does the hoofing catch fire here in the way that a dance show should.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this glitzy adaptation of Luhrmann's film. While some praise the dazzling choreography and infectious energy, others find it vapid and overstuffed, with the spectacle overwhelming the story's charm.
